summary: Discusses problems with maintaining large mailing lists, especially how error reports are processed. It is informational and describes issues rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When you send one letter to thousands of people, many come back undeliverable. This talks about how messy that is.

questions: why are large mailing lists hard to run
what is a mailing list sublist
what is a hard error versus a soft error in email
subtitle: What running the IETF mailing lists taught ISI about bounced mail, sublists and misdirected requests.

tldr.problem: Large mailing lists generate a steady stream of error reports, address changes and misdirected requests, and the people running them have to sort through all of it by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the work at USC-ISI, which kept about 25 lists, and walks through typical problems with real examples: errors sent to the wrong person, sublists with no owner, and requests sent to the wrong mailbox.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion document, not a protocol. It asks users to sort problems out locally and sublist owners to make sure error reports reach them.

today: RFC 1211 is an Informational memo from March 1991. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the RFC index data, and it records the authors' experience, not a standard.

sections.title: The Workload of a Large List
sections.content:
RFC 1211 is a discussion memo, not a specification. Most of its examples come from managing the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) mailing list, and the authors say most of the specific problems shown have already been corrected.

At USC Information Sciences Institute (ISI) the authors maintain lists for the Internet Research Groups, the IETF and other groups, about 25 lists in all. They receive about 400 messages a month asking to add or delete addresses, which is about 20 messages a day requesting changes. They also receive about 300 error messages a month from delivery problems. Many are duplicates, but about 10 cases per day need investigation.
sections.plainLanguage: Looking after a big club mailing list means answering lots of notes about changed addresses and lots of returned letters, every single day.

sections.title: Reading Error Reports
sections.content:
Many error reports are soft errors, mostly delayed delivery notices such as 'not delivered for 2 days, will try for 3 more days'. They waste the maintainer's time and are otherwise ignored, unless the same host keeps appearing for many days. Ignoring them is not always easy, because one message can report on several mailboxes and the hard errors must be picked out.

Hard errors such as 'no such user' need action. Often the answer is simply to delete the mailbox from the list, but if it belongs to someone known to be active, such as a working group chair, more digging is needed. 'No such host' may be temporary, but if it continues for several days it must be investigated.

Error conditions have no standardized names ('no such user' versus 'user unknown'), so it is hard to tell whether an error is soft or hard. The memo gives odd examples, such as a cryptic mail system error and 'Can't Find Mail Center!', and Appendix F collects a large sample of such messages for other maintainers.
sections.plainLanguage: Some returned letters just say 'we will try again', which you can ignore. Others say 'this person does not exist', and those need action. The trouble is that every post office words them differently.

sections.title: Investigating a Bad Address
sections.content:
The first step is to check whether the mailbox is on the list. If so, the maintainer checks whether there really is a problem, using the SMTP VRFY and EXPN features, Finger or Whois. This often shows the user has recently changed address, which has to be confirmed by exchanging messages (with the postmaster) before the list is updated.

If the user is not on the list, the mail probably goes through an exploder or sublist. The path in the error report's received lines usually shows which one, and EXPN can sometimes check it before the postmaster is told. If the host is unknown, the programs whathost, dig, ping and traceroute may find the problem, though fixing it may take talking to host and domain administrators.

If a problem cannot be resolved, the entry is deleted. That can lead to the reply 'I used to be on the ietf list, how come I am not getting the messages any more?' (Appendix A).
sections.plainLanguage: Like a detective, the maintainer follows the trail on the returned letter to find which office it passed through, then asks that office's helper to fix the address.

sections.title: Typical Problems
sections.content:
Misdirected error reports are the most frequent problem: errors go to the author of the message rather than the list owner. At ISI the SMTP 'from' information is added when the message is distributed so that compliant hosts send errors to the list owner, but not all hosts do this, and some ignore it.

Sublists are mailboxes whose alias expands to another list or group of recipients. The memo asks sublist maintainers to set up ownership, for example an owner-ietf-local alias, so errors reach them, but few people seem to understand list ownership. Many hosts do not implement EXPN or VRFY, so checks are inconclusive. Sublists in other mail worlds such as UUCP or BITNET are worse. When the recorded sublist owner has moved on, ISI falls back to the postmaster, though not every site has a postmaster mailbox.

Users also send requests and changes to the main list instead of the request mailbox, or send messages meant for the list to the request mailbox. In both cases the maintainers forward the message and tell the user the right address.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest mix-ups are returned letters going to the wrong person, small lists hidden inside the big list, and people dropping their notes into the wrong mailbox.

sections.title: Summary and Advice
sections.content:
Running a mailing list should be easy, and with small lists it is. As lists get large and traffic heavy, changes and errors grow to many a day, and the effort becomes significant. A further problem is the creativity of mail program developers in inventing so many different error reports.

The authors' advice is brief. Users should be considerate and try to work problems out locally. Sublist owners should do everything they can to get error messages for their sublist sent to them, and to get users on their system to talk to them about additions and deletions.

The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors ask everyone to be kind and to fix local problems locally, so the busy list keepers do not have to chase every one.
